title: Getting Field Crews to Code Job Costs Correctly
excerpt: Job cost reports are only as good as what the crew writes on a time sheet. Here is how to get coding right at the source rather than fixing it in the office.
metaDescription: How to get construction field crews coding job costs correctly — cost code structure, time entry habits, and fixing bad data at the source.
keywords: job cost coding, field time coding, construction cost codes, labor coding construction
body:
Your Job Cost Report Is Only as Good as a Time Sheet

Every job cost problem I get called in to fix traces back to the same place. Not the software. Not the chart of accounts. A time sheet where someone wrote "misc" in the cost code column because they were tired and it was Friday.

You can buy the best construction ERP on the market. If the foreman codes eight hours to the wrong phase, the report lies to you — and it lies confidently, in a nicely formatted PDF, which is worse than not having the report at all.

Why Crews Code Badly (It Is Usually Not Laziness)

Before blaming the field, look at what you are asking them to do. In most companies I review, the cost code list has grown to two or three hundred entries, most of them unused, several of them near-duplicates. A foreman standing in the rain at 4:40pm is being asked to pick between "03-3000 Concrete Placement" and "03-3100 Concrete — Place & Finish." He picks one. Next week he picks the other.

The common causes, in the order I find them:

  • Too many codes. If a crew uses fifteen codes on a typical job, a list of two hundred is noise.
  • Codes that overlap. Two codes that a reasonable person could read the same way will be used interchangeably. That is not a training problem, it is a design problem.
  • No feedback. The crew never sees what their coding produced. Data goes into a system and nothing ever comes back.
  • Coding after the fact. A time sheet filled in on Friday for the whole week is a work of fiction, not a record.

Cut the List Before You Train Anyone

Start by pulling last year's labor by cost code and sorting descending. In most contracting businesses, twenty codes carry 90% of the hours. Everything below that is either a genuine rarity or a code nobody understands.

Build a short list per work type. A framing crew does not need the sitework codes on their sheet. Give each crew the ten or twelve codes they actually use, printed on the time sheet or preloaded in the app, and route the rest through the office as exceptions.

Then write a one-line definition for each code in plain language — the kind you would say out loud. "Anything to do with setting or stripping forms" beats a CSI division reference nobody reads.

Make the Right Answer the Easy Answer

Crews code correctly when correct coding is the path of least resistance. Practically that means:

  • Code at the point of work, not at the end of the week. Daily entry, on a phone, takes ninety seconds and is roughly accurate. Weekly recall is neither.
  • Pre-populate what you can. The job number, the crew, the date — none of that should be typed by hand.
  • Limit the picker to the job's actual budget lines. If a code has no budget on that job, it should not appear as an option without a deliberate override.
  • Force a note on anything coded to "other". Not to punish anyone, but so the office can recode it properly instead of guessing.

Close the Loop So the Field Sees Why It Matters

This is the step almost everyone skips, and it does more than any training session. Once a month, show each foreman their own jobs: budgeted hours against actual by code. Not as a performance review — as information.

The first time a foreman sees that his excavation came in 40 hours under while his backfill ran 60 over, two things happen. He gets interested in the numbers, and he starts caring whether the hours landed in the right bucket. You cannot train that into someone. You can only show it to them.

Fixing Bad Data Without Destroying the History

When you find miscoded hours, resist the urge to quietly adjust them into the right place and move on. Post a correcting entry with a reference to the original, so the audit trail survives. If you are restating a period that has already been reported to a lender or a surety, note it — restating history without a record is how contractors lose credibility with the people who fund them.

And track how much recoding you are doing. If the office is correcting 15% of labor lines every week, the problem is upstream and no amount of correcting will fix it. That is a signal to go back to the code list.

What Good Looks Like

You know the system is working when the office is recoding under 2% of labor lines, foremen are asking about their numbers rather than being chased for time sheets, and the WIP schedule can be produced without anyone querying whether the costs are in the right jobs.

That is not a software outcome. It is a design and habit outcome, and it is usually two weeks of work to get there.
